title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{3}
Let $\nu,s\in\mathbb C$, let $f\in L^2(S,L^S_{\nu;s})$, and put
$F=P_{\nu,s}f$.  Then

\begin{center}
\small
\renewcommand{1.5}{1.5}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.34\textwidth}p{0.60\textwidth}@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Parameter} & \textbf{Conclusion}\\
\hline

\(\displaystyle s+\nu=\frac{2n}{r}\)
&
\(F\) is holomorphic.
\\
\hline

\(\displaystyle s=\nu,\quad
\nu\ne\frac nr,\quad \nu\notin-\mathbb N_0\)
&
\(\displaystyle
F\in
C^{\max\{0,\lceil\frac nr-\operatorname{Re}\nu\rceil\}}
(\overline\Omega,L^\Omega_\nu)
\Longrightarrow
F\text{ is holomorphic}.
\)
\\
\hline

\(\displaystyle s=\nu\in-\mathbb N_0\)
&
\(\displaystyle
F\in
\begin{cases}
\mathcal R^{\frac nr-\nu}(\overline\Omega,L^\Omega_\nu),
&\Omega\text{ is of tube type},\\
C^{b+1-\nu}(\overline\Omega,L^\Omega_\nu),
&\Omega\text{ is non-tube}
\end{cases}
\Longrightarrow
\bar\partial\mathbb D_{-\nu,0}F=0.
\)
\\
\hline

\(\displaystyle
\frac nr-\frac{s+\nu}{2}\in\mathbb N,\quad
\frac nr-\frac{s-\nu}{2}\in-\mathbb N_0
\)
&
\(\displaystyle
\mathbb D_{
\frac{s-\nu}{2}-\frac nr,\,
\frac nr-\frac{s+\nu}{2}}F=0.
\)
\\
\hline

\(\displaystyle
-\frac{s+\nu}{2}\in\mathbb N_0,\quad
\frac{s-\nu}{2}\in\mathbb N,\quad
\frac nr-\frac{s-\nu}{2}\notin-\mathbb N_0
\)
&
\(\displaystyle
F\in
\mathcal R^{\frac nr-\frac{s+\nu}{2}}
(\overline\Omega,L^\Omega_\nu)
\Longrightarrow
\mathbb D_{
-\frac{s+\nu}{2},\,
\frac{s-\nu}{2}}F=0.
\)
\\
\hline

All remaining parameters
&
There exists $m\in\mathbb N_0$ such that
\(\displaystyle
F\in C^m(\overline\Omega,L^\Omega_\nu)
\Longrightarrow F=0.
\)
\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{4} Let $F\in C^{2}(\Omega)$ be Bergman-harmonic. If
\[
F\in 
\begin{cases}
\mathcal{R}^{\frac nr}(\overline\Omega), & \Omega\text{ is of tube
type},\\[1mm] 
C^{b+1}(\overline\Omega), & \Omega\text{ is non-tube},
\end{cases}
\]
then $F$ is pluriharmonic.

name: Graham type Theorem

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Upmeier's description of conical polynomials
\cite[Section~4, formula~(4.2) and the following paragraph]{UpmeierKinv}
implies that $\mathcal P_{(q)}$ is spanned by
$\ell_c^q$, where $c$ ranges over minimal tripotents.
Every rank-one $\xi$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of such a $c$,
so the polynomials $\ell_\xi^q$ also span $\mathcal P_{(q)}$.

By \eqref{14}, $\ell_\xi^q/q!$ represents evaluation at
$\xi$ on the full space of homogeneous polynomials of degree
$q$. It also lies in $\mathcal P_{(q)}$, so it represents
evaluation on that subspace. This gives \eqref{17}.
Taking Fischer adjoints gives the statement about
$\partial_\xi^q$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{16}, $p$ is a linear combination of $\ell_\xi^q$
with $\xi$ of rank one. Since
$\partial_j\ell_\xi^q=q\overline{\xi_j}\ell_\xi^{q-1}$,
the same spanning statement gives
$\partial_jp\in\mathcal P_{(q-1)}$.
For any homogeneous holomorphic polynomial $u$ of degree $q-1$,
Fischer adjointness, orthogonality of the polynomial $K$-types,
and \eqref{15} give
\[
\langle z_ju,p\rangle_S
=\frac{\langle z_ju,p\rangle_F}{(n/r)_q}
=\frac{\langle u,\partial_jp\rangle_F}{(n/r)_q}
=\frac{\langle u,\partial_jp\rangle_S}{n/r+q-1}.
\]
For $u$ of any other homogeneous degree, both sides vanish.
Since polynomials are dense in $H^2(S)$, this identifies the
adjoint of multiplication by $z_j$ at $p$ with
$\partial_jp/(n/r+q-1)$. The adjoint is also
$\Pi_H(p\bar z_j|_S)$, proving \eqref{22}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{28}
Let $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$ and put $g=\pi(\widetilde g)$.
The map $g$ and its complex Jacobian extend holomorphically to
a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, where the Jacobian does
not vanish. Every complex power specified by $\widetilde g$
extends to a possibly smaller neighborhood. Near the identity
in $\widetilde G$, the extensions can be chosen on a common
neighborhood and depend smoothly on $\widetilde g$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the Harish--Chandra realization, $\Omega$ lies in an affine
chart of its compact dual. The action of $g$ extends to an
automorphism of the compact dual
\cite[Chapter~VIII, Corollary~7.15]{Helgason}.
Because $g(\overline\Omega)=\overline\Omega$, this action and
its inverse are holomorphic near $\overline\Omega$ in the same
affine chart. Thus the Jacobian is nonzero there after the
neighborhood is made smaller.

The closed domain $\overline\Omega$ is convex, so we can choose
a convex neighborhood within the region where the Jacobian is
nonzero. Any two holomorphic logarithms of the Jacobian on $\Omega$
differ by a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$. We choose the
constant in the logarithm on this neighborhood so that its
restriction to $\Omega$ is the branch specified by
$\widetilde g$. Exponentiation then extends the chosen
complex powers.

The compact-dual action depends smoothly on the group element.
Compactness of $\overline\Omega$ gives a common neighborhood for
$\widetilde g$ near the identity. After shrinking it, the
Jacobians are uniformly close to $1$, so their logarithms and
complex powers also depend smoothly on $\widetilde g$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{29}
Let $\sigma,\theta\in\mathbb C$, $f\in L^2(S)$, and
$F=P_{\sigma,\theta}f$. If $F\in C^m(\overline\Omega)$,
where $m\in\mathbb N_0$, then
$P_{\sigma,\theta}\pi_{\sigma,\theta}(\widetilde g)f$
and $P_{\sigma,\theta}\Pi_\tau^S f$ also belong to
$C^m(\overline\Omega)$ for every $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$
and every $K$-type $\tau$. The same holds for
$C^{m,\varepsilon}$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$, and for
$\mathcal R^q$, $q>0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Equation~\eqref{27} expresses the first transform as a
holomorphic, nonvanishing Jacobian factor times $F\circ g^{-1}$.
By Lemma~\ref{28}, the map $g^{-1}$ and the Jacobian
factor extend smoothly to a neighborhood of
$\overline\Omega$. Composition and multiplication
therefore preserve the stated $C^m$ and H\"older regularity.

For the projection, \eqref{11} gives
$P_{\sigma,\theta}\Pi_\tau^S f=\Pi_\tau^\Omega F$.
Choose a $K$-invariant neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$ on
which $F$ has an extension. Since $K$ is compact and acts
linearly, the functions $F\circ k^{-1}$ have uniform $C^m$
and, when applicable, $C^{m,\varepsilon}$ bounds on a smaller
such neighborhood. Integrating them against the character in
the definition of $\Pi_\tau^\Omega$ preserves these bounds.
The claim for $\mathcal R^q$ follows from its definition.

title: Definition
body_md:
For
$F\in C^q(\Omega)$, define the $\mathcal W_q^\vee$-valued
function $\mathcal D_qF$ by
\[
(\mathcal D_qF(z))(p^*)=p^*(\partial)F(z),
\qquad p\in\mathcal P_{(q)}.
\]
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{32}
For $L\in\mathbb N_0$ and $F\in\operatorname{Pol}(V)$,
$\mathcal D_{L+1}F$ vanishes on $\Omega$ if and only if
$F\in\mathcal F_L$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, $\mathcal D_{L+1}F\equiv0$ if and only if
$p^*(\partial)F=0$ for every $p\in\mathcal P_{(L+1)}$.
For such $p$ and any $R\in\operatorname{Pol}(V)$, Fischer
adjointness gives
\[
\langle pR,F\rangle_F
=\langle R,p^*(\partial)F\rangle_F.
\]
Consequently, $\mathcal D_{L+1}F\equiv0$ implies
$F\perp\mathcal P_{(L+1)}\operatorname{Pol}(V)$.
Conversely, suppose that
$F\perp\mathcal P_{(L+1)}\operatorname{Pol}(V)$.
For each $p\in\mathcal P_{(L+1)}$, the function
$p^*(\partial)F$ is a polynomial. Taking
$R=p^*(\partial)F$ in the displayed identity gives
\[
\|p^*(\partial)F\|_F^2
=\langle p\,p^*(\partial)F,F\rangle_F=0.
\]
Thus $p^*(\partial)F=0$ for every such $p$, which means
$\mathcal D_{L+1}F\equiv0$.
By \eqref{30}, the orthogonal complement of
$\mathcal P_{(L+1)}\operatorname{Pol}(V)$ is
$\bigoplus_{\alpha_1\le L}\mathcal P_\alpha=\mathcal F_L$. The proof is complete.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote the span on the right of \eqref{31} by $W_L$.
Because $\alpha$ is a partition,
$(-L)_\alpha\ne0$ exactly when $\alpha_1\le L$.
Formula~\eqref{13} gives the finite expansion
\[
h(\,\cdot\,,w)^L
=\sum_{\alpha_1\le L}(-L)_\alpha
K_\alpha^F(\,\cdot\,,w),
\qquad w\in\Omega.
\]
Thus $W_L\subset\mathcal F_L$. Suppose that
$p=\sum_{\alpha_1\le L}p_\alpha\in\mathcal F_L$
is Fischer-orthogonal to $W_L$. By the reproducing
property of $K_\alpha^F$, for every $w\in\Omega$,
\[
0=\langle p,h(\,\cdot\,,w)^L\rangle_F
 =\sum_{\alpha_1\le L}(-L)_\alpha p_\alpha(w).
\]
The polynomial on the right vanishes on $\Omega$, hence
identically equals to $0$ on $V$. Its terms belong to distinct spaces
$\mathcal P_\alpha$, so each $(-L)_\alpha p_\alpha=0$.
All these coefficients are nonzero; thus $p=0$.
Since $\mathcal F_L$ is finite-dimensional,
$W_L=\mathcal F_L$, proving \eqref{31}.
head: environment

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$ and $z\in\Omega$, and put
\(y=g^{-1}z\) and \(A=(g^{-1})'(z)\).
By Lemma~\ref{16}, $\mathcal W_{L+1}$ is spanned by
$\varphi_\xi=(\ell_\xi^{L+1})^*$ with $\xi$ of rank one.
The definition of $\mathcal D_{L+1}$ gives
\[
\bigl(\mathcal D_{L+1}F(y)\bigr)(\varphi_\xi)
=\partial_\xi^{L+1}F(y).
\]
The product and chain rules give
\[
\partial_\xi^{L+1}\!\left[
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}^{-L/p_\Omega}(F\circ g^{-1})
\right](z)
=J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-L/p_\Omega}
\partial_{A\xi}^{L+1}F(y)+R_{\xi,z}(F),
\]
where $R_{\xi,z}(F)$ depends only on derivatives of $F$ at $y$
of order at most $L$. Since
$C_g(z)\varphi_\xi=\varphi_{A\xi}$, the first term on the right is
\[
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-L/p_\Omega}
\bigl(B_g(z)\mathcal D_{L+1}F(y)\bigr)(\varphi_\xi).
\]
The $\varphi_\xi$ span $\mathcal W_{L+1}$, so the difference
in \eqref{34} involves only $\partial^\gamma F(y)$,
$|\gamma|\le L$.

The space $\mathcal F_L$ is invariant under \(F\longmapsto J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}^{-L/p_\Omega} (F\circ g^{-1})\).
Indeed, by \eqref{24},
\[
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-L/p_\Omega}
h(g^{-1}z,w)^L
=
\overline{
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(gw)
}^{\,L/p_\Omega}
h(z,gw)^L,
\]
and the assertion follows from \eqref{31}.

For $P\in\mathcal F_L$, the invariance just proved shows
that its weighted pullback also belongs to $\mathcal F_L$.
Lemma~\ref{32} therefore makes both sides of \eqref{34}
zero. Hence $R_{\xi,z}(P)=0$ for every $P\in\mathcal F_L$.

For a general $F$, define
\[
P_y(w)=\sum_{|\gamma|\le L}
\frac{\partial^\gamma F(y)}{\gamma!}(w-y)^\gamma.
\]
This polynomial has total degree at most $L$, so
$P_y\in\mathcal F_L$. By construction,
\[
\partial^\gamma P_y(y)=\partial^\gamma F(y),
\qquad |\gamma|\le L.
\]
Since $R_{\xi,z}$ depends only on these derivatives,
\[
R_{\xi,z}(F)=R_{\xi,z}(P_y)=0.
\]
Thus \eqref{34} holds after evaluation on every
$\varphi_\xi$. They span $\mathcal W_{L+1}$,
so \eqref{34} holds in $\mathcal W_{L+1}^\vee$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{35}
Let $L=\sigma-\frac nr\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$F=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f$ for $f\in L^2(S)$.
For $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$, put
$F_{\widetilde g}=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}
(\pi_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\widetilde g)f)$.
If $\bigl(\bar\partial(\mathcal D_{L+1}F_{\widetilde g})\bigr)_0=0$
for every $\widetilde g$, then
$\bar\partial(\mathcal D_{L+1}F)=0$ on $\Omega$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $g=\pi(\widetilde g)$. By \eqref{27} and
$L=\sigma-\frac nr$,
\[
F_{\widetilde g}(z)
=
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-L/p_\Omega}
F(g^{-1}z).
\]
Equation~\eqref{34} therefore gives
\[
\mathcal D_{L+1}F_{\widetilde g}(z)
=
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-L/p_\Omega}
B_g(z)
\bigl(\mathcal D_{L+1}F\bigr)(g^{-1}z).
\]
Differentiating under the integral in \eqref{8} shows
that the transforms are smooth on $\Omega$. The Jacobian
factor and $B_g(z)$ are holomorphic in $z$.
Taking an antiholomorphic derivative at $0$ and using the
hypothesis gives
\[
 0
=
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(0)^{-L/p_\Omega}
B_g(0)
\circ
\bigl(\bar\partial(\mathcal D_{L+1}F)\bigr)_{g^{-1}0}
\circ
\overline{(g^{-1})'(0)}.
\]
The Jacobian factor is nonzero, and both
$B_g(0)$ and $(g^{-1})'(0)$ are invertible. Hence
$\bigl(\bar\partial(\mathcal D_{L+1}F)\bigr)_{g^{-1}0}=0$.
Since $G$ acts transitively on $\Omega$, the result follows.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{37}
Let $L,j_0\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $F$ be the scalar representative
of a $C^{L+1}$ section of
$L^\Omega_{-(L+j_0)}$. For $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$,
put $g=\pi(\widetilde g)$ and
$F_{\widetilde g}=T_{-(L+j_0)}(\widetilde g)F$, as in
\eqref{6}. Then, as an identity in $\mathcal W_{L+1}^\vee$,
\begin{equation}\label{38}
\mathbb D_{L,j_0}F_{\widetilde g}(z)
=
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(z)^{-(L+j_0)/p_\Omega}
B_g(z)
(\mathbb D_{L,j_0}F)(g^{-1}z).
\end{equation}

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Combining \cite[Theorems~6.2 and~6.3, formulas~(6.20) and~(6.22)]{Koranyi}
and using $\ell=\theta-\sigma$ and
$s=2n/r-\sigma-\theta$, we obtain, in the scalar trivialization,
\begin{equation}\label{388}
h(z,z)^{\sigma-\theta}
\sum_{i,j}b^{i\bar j}(z)
\partial_i\left(
h(z,z)^{-(\sigma-\theta)}
\bar\partial_jF
\right)
+
r\sigma\left(\frac nr-\theta\right)F
=0.
\end{equation}
Taking the complex conjugate of \cite[formula~(46)]{EYZ}
and using our notation for the Bergman operator gives
\[
\bar\partial(-\log h(z,z))
=
B(z,\bar z)^{-1}(z-Q(z)\bar z).
\]
Since $B(z,\bar z)$ is Hermitian,
\[
\sum_i
b^{i\bar j}(z)\partial_i\log h(z,z)
=
-\overline{(z-Q(z)\bar z)_j}.
\]
Expanding \eqref{388} and using the preceding identity gives
\eqref{41}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $c$ be a minimal tripotent and put
$\ell_c(z)=\langle z,c\rangle$. For $0\le t<1$ and $\omega\in S$,
\begin{equation}\label{42}
h(\omega,tc)=1-t\ell_c(\omega),\qquad
h(tc,\omega)=1-t\overline{\ell_c(\omega)},\qquad
h(tc,tc)=1-t^2.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $m\ge0$, \eqref{14} and \eqref{17}, together with
the direct-sum decomposition \eqref{10}, give
$K_\alpha^F(z,c)=0$ when $|\alpha|=m$ and $\alpha\ne(m)$.
Thus \eqref{13} with $u=-1$ gives, for $z\in\Omega$,
\[
h(z,tc)
=\sum_{m\ge0}(-1)_m t^mK_{(m)}^F(z,c)
=1-t\ell_c(z).
\]
Both sides are polynomials in $z$, so the identity holds
on $V$. Taking $z=\omega$ gives the first identity in
\eqref{42}. The second follows from
$h(tc,\omega)=\overline{h(\omega,tc)}$.
Taking $z=tc$ and using $\langle c,c\rangle=1$
gives the third.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{42},
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
=
(1-t^2)^\sigma
\int_S
(1-t\overline{\ell_c})^{-\theta}
(1-t\ell_c)^{-\sigma}\ell_c^q\,du.
\]
Expanding the two factors and using \eqref{389} gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
=
(1-t^2)^\sigma t^q
\sum_{m\ge0}
\frac{(\theta)_{m+q}(\sigma)_m}
     {(\frac nr)_{m+q}m!}\,t^{2m}.
\]
Factoring out $(\theta)_q/(\frac nr)_q$ and using the
definition of ${}_2F_1$ proves \eqref{44}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Setting $q=0$ in \eqref{44} gives
\begin{equation}\label{45}
P_{\sigma,\theta}1(tc)
=
(1-t^2)^\sigma
{}_2F_1\left(
\sigma,\theta;\frac nr;t^2
\right).
\end{equation}

The kernel in \eqref{8} also gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}\overline f
=
h(z,z)^{\sigma-\theta}
\overline{P_{\bar\theta,\bar\sigma}f}.
\]
Applying \eqref{44} with $q=1$ and parameters
$(\bar\theta,\bar\sigma)$ therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{46}
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\overline{\ell_c})(tc)
=
\frac{r\sigma}{n}\,
t(1-t^2)^\sigma
{}_2F_1\left(
\theta,\sigma+1;\frac nr+1;t^2
\right).
\end{equation}

Finally, Euler's transformation rewrites \eqref{44} as
\begin{equation}\label{47}
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
=
\frac{(\theta)_q}{(\frac nr)_q}
t^q(1-t^2)^{\frac nr-\theta}
{}_2F_1\left(
\frac nr+q-\sigma,\frac nr-\theta;
\frac nr+q;t^2
\right).
\end{equation}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{48}
Let $C>0$ and $A,B\in\mathbb C$.  The function \[\psi(\rho) = \rho^A{}_2F_1(A,B;C;1-\rho), \quad 0<\rho\le1,\]
extends smoothly across $\rho=0$ if and only if at least one of
\begin{equation}\label{49}
A=0;\qquad
B=C;\qquad
A\in\mathbb N_0,\ B\in-\mathbb N_0;\qquad
A-C\in\mathbb N_0,\ C-B\in\mathbb N_0
\end{equation}
holds.  In each of these cases $\psi$ is a polynomial in $\rho$.  Otherwise
$\psi$ fails to have a $C^m$ extension at $0$ for some
$m\in\mathbb N_0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The four alternatives in \eqref{49} are sufficient. If $A=0$ or
$B=C$, then $\psi=1$. In the third case the Gauss series
terminates. In the fourth case Euler's transformation gives
\[
\psi(\rho)=
\rho^{C-B}{}_2F_1(C-A,C-B;C;1-\rho),
\]
which is again a polynomial.

Conversely, suppose that $\psi$ is smooth at $\rho=0$.
The Gauss hypergeometric equation gives
\[
\rho(1-\rho)\psi''
+\bigl(B+1-A-C+(A-B-1)\rho\bigr)\psi'
+\frac{A(C-B)}{\rho}\psi=0.
\]
Its only possible singularities are $0$, $1$, and $\infty$,
all regular. The Frobenius expansions show that smoothness
at $0$ forces $\psi$ to be analytic there; see
\cite[Section~2.7(i)]{DLMF}.
The defining series shows that $\psi$ is also analytic at $1$.
Continuation around both finite singularities is therefore
trivial, so $\psi$ extends to an entire function.

The point at infinity is a regular singularity. Its Frobenius
expansions therefore give constants $C_0,M>0$ such that
$|\psi(\rho)|\leq C_0(1+|\rho|)^M$ for large $|\rho|$.
For any integer $n>M$, Cauchy's estimate on $|\rho|=R$ gives
\[
|\psi^{(n)}(0)|
\leq \frac{n!C_0(1+R)^M}{R^n}.
\]
Letting $R\to\infty$ shows that $\psi^{(n)}(0)=0$.
Hence $\psi$ is a polynomial.

If $\psi$ is constant, then $\psi(1)=1$ and the equation gives
$A=0$ or $B=C$. Otherwise, let $N\geq1$ be its degree and
$m\geq0$ its order of vanishing at $0$. Comparing the
highest and lowest powers of $\rho$ gives
\[
N=A-B,\qquad (m-A)(m-C+B)=0.
\]
Since $0\leq m\leq N$, either
$A=m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $B=m-N\in-\mathbb N_0$, or
$C-B=m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $A-C=N-m\in\mathbb N_0$.
These are the remaining two conditions in \eqref{49}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{50}
Let $\sigma,\theta\in\mathbb C$, let
$m\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, and let $f\in L^2(S)$.  If \[0\ne P_{\sigma,\theta}f\in C^m(\overline\Omega),\]
then $P_{\sigma,\theta}1\in C^m(\overline\Omega)$.  If
$m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$, the same statement holds with
$C^m$ replaced by $C^{m,\varepsilon}$.  For every $s>0$, it also holds with
$C^m$ replaced by $\mathcal R^s$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F=P_{\sigma,\theta}f$ and choose $z_0\in\Omega$ with $F(z_0)\ne0$.
Choose $g\in G$ with $g^{-1}0=z_0$ and choose a lift
$\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$.  Put
\[
 f_{\widetilde g}=\pi_{\sigma,\theta}(\widetilde g)f,
 \qquad
 F_{\widetilde g}=P_{\sigma,\theta}f_{\widetilde g}.
\]
By \eqref{27}, \(F_{\widetilde g}(0) =J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(0)^{(\theta-\sigma)/p_\Omega}F(z_0)\),
so $F_{\widetilde g}(0)\ne0$.  Lemma~\ref{29} gives the same boundary
regularity for $F_{\widetilde g}$ as for $F$. When $m=\infty$, both
uses of Lemma~\ref{29} in this proof are made at every finite order.

Let \(f_0=\int_K f_{\widetilde g}\circ k^{-1}\,dk\).
Since $K$ acts transitively on $S$, and $h(0,\omega)=h(\omega,0)=1$,
\[
f_0(w)=\int_S f_{\widetilde g}(\omega)\,du(\omega)
=F_{\widetilde g}(0),\qquad w\in S.
\]

Since $P_{\sigma,\theta}$ intertwines the $K$-actions,
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}f_0
=\int_K F_{\widetilde g}(k^{-1}z)\,dk.
\]
As $f_0\equiv F_{\widetilde g}(0)$, we obtain
\[
F_{\widetilde g}(0)P_{\sigma,\theta}1
=\int_K F_{\widetilde g}(k^{-1}z)\,dk.
\]
The right-hand side is the $K$-average of $F_{\widetilde g}$ and therefore
has the same $C^m$, $C^{m,\varepsilon}$, or $\mathcal R^s$ boundary
regularity; see Lemma~\ref{29}. Since $F_{\widetilde g}(0)\ne0$,
$P_{\sigma,\theta}1$ has the same regularity.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{51}
Let $\sigma,\theta\in\mathbb C$.  If \(P_{\sigma,\theta}(L^2(S)) \cap C^\infty(\overline\Omega)\ne\{0\}\),
then at least one of the following holds:
\begin{equation}\label{52}
\sigma=0;\qquad
\theta=\frac nr;\qquad
\sigma\in\mathbb N_0,\ \theta\in-\mathbb N_0;\qquad
\sigma-\frac nr\in\mathbb N_0,\ 
\frac nr-\theta\in\mathbb N_0.
\end{equation}

At every parameter outside \eqref{52}, there exists
$m\in\mathbb N_0$ such that, for every $f\in L^2(S)$,
\begin{equation}\label{53}
P_{\sigma,\theta}f\in C^m(\overline\Omega)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
P_{\sigma,\theta}f=0.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $P_{\sigma,\theta}f$ is nonzero and smooth on
$\overline\Omega$.  By Lemma~\ref{50},
$P_{\sigma,\theta}1$ has the same regularity.  For a minimal tripotent $c$, \eqref{45} gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}1(tc)
=
(1-t^2)^\sigma
{}_2F_1\left(
\sigma,\theta;\frac nr;t^2
\right).
\]
Putting $\rho=1-t^2$ and applying Lemma~\ref{48} with \(A=\sigma,\quad B=\theta,\quad C=\frac nr\)
gives exactly the four alternatives in \eqref{52}.

Now suppose that $(\sigma,\theta)$ lies outside
\eqref{52}.  Lemma~\ref{48} shows that the
preceding radial function fails to have a $C^m$ extension at $t=1$ for
some finite $m\in\mathbb N_0$.  If a nonzero
$P_{\sigma,\theta}f$ belonged to $C^m(\overline\Omega)$, then
Lemma~\ref{50} would give the same regularity for
$P_{\sigma,\theta}1$, a contradiction.  Hence
\eqref{53} holds.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\sigma=0$, then \(P_{0,\theta}f(z) = \int_S h(z,\omega)^{-\theta}f(\omega)\,du(\omega)\),
which is holomorphic in $z$.

For the second assertion, we recall that
\[
h(z,z)^{-m}P_{m,-q}f(z)
=
\int_S h(z,\omega)^q h(\omega,z)^{-m}f(\omega)\,du(\omega).
\]
By \eqref{31}, $h(\,\cdot\,,w)^q\in\mathcal F_q$
for $w\in\Omega$. Since $\mathcal F_q$ is finite-dimensional,
letting $w\to\omega\in S$ gives
$h(\,\cdot\,,\omega)^q\in\mathcal F_q$.
Hence Lemma~\ref{32} gives \(\mathcal D_{q+1,z}h(z,\omega)^q=0\).
The operator $\mathcal D_{q+1}$ contains only holomorphic derivatives, while
$h(\omega,z)^{-m}$ is antiholomorphic in $z$. On every compact subset of
$\Omega$, the kernel and all derivatives occurring here are bounded
uniformly in $\omega\in S$. Since $f\in L^2(S)\subset L^1(S)$, we may
differentiate under the integral, obtaining \eqref{55}.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\mu\notin\mathbb Z$, the connection formula
\cite[formula~(15.8.4)]{DLMF}, with the normalization
\cite[formula~(15.1.2)]{DLMF}, gives
\[
{}_2F_1(\lambda-\mu,1;\lambda+1;1-\rho)
=\frac{\lambda}{\mu}
{}_2F_1(\lambda-\mu,1;1-\mu;\rho)
+\frac{\Gamma(\lambda+1)\Gamma(-\mu)}
       {\Gamma(\lambda-\mu)}
\rho^\mu(1-\rho)^{-\lambda}.
\]
The first term is analytic at $\rho=0$. For $\mu\in-\mathbb N$,
$1-\mu,\lambda-\mu>0$, so both parameter limits are finite
and the identity remains valid. For $\mu\in\mathbb N$,
\cite[formula~(15.8.10)]{DLMF} gives the logarithmic term
with an analytic remainder. Finally, $\Gamma$ has no zeros,
and the assumption on $\lambda-\mu$ keeps the denominator finite.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{56}
Let $\sigma\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and
$\sigma-\frac{n}{r}\notin\mathbb N_0$.  Put \(M=\max\{0,\lceil\operatorname{Re}\sigma\rceil\}\).
If $f\in L^2(S)$ and
$F=P_{\sigma,\frac{n}{r}}f\in C^M(\overline\Omega)$, then $F$ is holomorphic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=\overline{\mathcal P_{(1)}}|_S$, and let $f_E$ be the orthogonal
projection of $f$ onto $E$. By the uniqueness statement following
\eqref{12}, $\mathcal P_{(1)}|_S$ occurs with multiplicity one in $L^2(S)$.
Complex conjugation preserves multiplicities, so $E$ is the full
$K$-isotypic component of its type. Lemma~\ref{29} gives
$P_{\sigma,n/r}f_E\in C^M(\overline\Omega)$. Since $P_{\sigma,n/r}$
intertwines the $K$-actions and $K$ preserves $C^M(\overline\Omega)$,
the space
\[
\{v\in E:P_{\sigma,n/r}v\in C^M(\overline\Omega)\}
\]
is $K$-invariant. If $f_E\ne0$, irreducibility of $E$ makes this space
equal to $E$.

By Lemma~\ref{16}, $\overline{\ell_c}|_S\in E$ for every minimal tripotent
$c$. If $f_E\ne0$, it follows that
$$P_{\sigma,n/r}(\overline{\ell_c})\in C^M(\overline\Omega).$$
We test this regularity on the radius $z=tc$. Put $\rho=1-t^2$.
By \eqref{46} and Euler's transformation
\cite[formula~(15.8.1)]{DLMF},
\[
P_{\sigma,n/r}(\overline{\ell_c})(tc)
=\frac{r\sigma}{n}\sqrt{1-\rho}\,
{}_2F_1\left(\frac nr-\sigma,1;\frac nr+1;1-\rho\right).
\]
The hypothesis $\sigma-\frac nr\notin\mathbb N_0$ gives
$\frac nr-\sigma\notin-\mathbb N_0$.
Lemma~\ref{551}, with $\lambda=\frac nr$ and $\mu=\sigma$,
gives the following expansion near $\rho=0$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
{}_2F_1\left(\frac nr-\sigma,1;\frac nr+1;1-\rho\right)
={}&H(\rho)+(1-\rho)^{-n/r}
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{\Gamma(\frac nr+1)\Gamma(-\sigma)}
     {\Gamma(\frac nr-\sigma)}\,\rho^\sigma,
&\sigma\notin\mathbb N_0,\\[3mm]
\displaystyle
\frac{(-1)^{\sigma+1}\Gamma(\frac nr+1)}
     {\sigma!\,\Gamma(\frac nr-\sigma)}
     \,\rho^\sigma\log\rho,
&\sigma\in\mathbb N.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $H$ is analytic near $\rho=0$, and both displayed coefficients
are nonzero.

Since $(1-\rho)^{-n/r}$ and $\sqrt{1-\rho}$ are analytic
and nonzero at $\rho=0$, hence they do not remove the singularity
found above. If $\sigma\notin\mathbb N_0$ and
$\operatorname{Re}\sigma\le0$, then $M=0$ and $\rho^\sigma$ has no
finite limit at $0$. If $\sigma\notin\mathbb N_0$ and
$\operatorname{Re}\sigma>0$, the $M$-th derivative of $\rho^\sigma$
has a nonzero leading term proportional to $\rho^{\sigma-M}$,
which has no finite limit. Finally, if $\sigma\in\mathbb N$, then
$M=\sigma$ and the $M$-th derivative of $\rho^\sigma\log\rho$
diverges. Since $\rho=1-t^2$ is a smooth coordinate near $t=1$,
$P_{\sigma,n/r}(\overline{\ell_c})(tc)$ cannot be $C^M$ there.
This contradicts the regularity obtained from $f_E\ne0$, so
$f_E=0$.

Thus $f\perp\overline{\mathcal P_{(1)}}|_S$, or equivalently,
\[
\int_S f(\omega)p(\omega)\,du(\omega)=0
\qquad (p\in\mathcal P_{(1)}).
\]
By \eqref{9}, $h(0,0)=1$ and
$\bar\partial h(z,z)|_{z=0}=0$. Differentiating \eqref{20}
at $z=0$, only the terms with $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=(1)$
contribute to the antiholomorphic derivative. Thus
\[
\bar\partial F(0)
=
\sigma\sum_i
\left(\int_S f(\omega)p_{(1),i}(\omega)\,du(\omega)\right)
\bar\partial\overline{p_{(1),i}}(0)
=0.
\]
Now let $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$, put $g=\pi(\widetilde g)$, and set \(F_{\widetilde g} = P_{\sigma,n/r} \pi_{\sigma,n/r}(\widetilde g)f\).
By Lemma~\ref{29}, $F_{\widetilde g}$ has the same boundary regularity,
so the preceding argument gives \(\bar\partial F_{\widetilde g}(0)=0\).
Formula~\eqref{27}
and the chain rule then give
$\bar\partial F(g^{-1}0)=0$: the Jacobian factor is
holomorphic and nonzero, and $(g^{-1})'(0)$ is invertible.
As $G$ acts transitively on $\Omega$, we obtain
$\bar\partial F=0$ on $\Omega$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{57}
Let $\sigma,\theta\in\mathbb C$ satisfy
\[
\sigma-\frac nr\in\mathbb N_0,
\qquad
\frac nr-\theta\in\mathbb N,
\qquad
\theta\notin-\mathbb N_0.
\]
If $f\in L^2(S)$ and \(F=P_{\sigma,\theta}f \in\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega)\),
then
\begin{equation}\label{58}
\mathcal D_{\sigma-\frac nr+1}
\left(
h(z,z)^{\theta-\frac nr}F
\right)=0.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put
\[
q=\sigma-\frac nr+1\in\mathbb N,
\qquad
j_0=\frac nr-\theta\in\mathbb N,
\qquad
H(z)=h(z,z)^{-j_0}F(z).
\]
We have $H=h(z,z)^{\sigma-j_0}(h(z,z)^{-\sigma}F)$.
Since $h(z,w)$ is antiholomorphic in $w$ and $h(z,0)=1$,
for every nonzero multi-index $\gamma$,
\[
\left.\partial_z^\gamma h(z,z)^{\sigma-j_0}\right|_{z=0}
=\left.\partial_z^\gamma h(z,0)^{\sigma-j_0}\right|_{z=0}
=0.
\]
Also $h(0,0)^{\sigma-j_0}=1$. The product rule therefore gives
$$p^*(\partial)H(0)=p^*(\partial)(h(z,z)^{-\sigma}F)(0)\ \
\mbox{for every}\  p\in\mathcal P_{(q)}.$$
Apply $p^*(\partial)$ to \eqref{20} and evaluate at $z=0$.
Terms with $\beta\ne0$ vanish because they still contain
$\bar z$. For the terms with $\beta=0$, the definition of the
Fischer inner product gives
\[
p^*(\partial)p_{\alpha,i}(0)
=\langle p_{\alpha,i},p\rangle_F.
\]
This vanishes unless $\alpha=(q)$, since
$p\in\mathcal P_{(q)}$ and the spaces $\mathcal P_\alpha$
are Fischer-orthogonal. For $\alpha=(q)$, expansion in the
Fischer-orthonormal basis gives
\[
\sum_i\langle p_{(q),i},p\rangle_F
\overline{p_{(q),i}(\omega)}=\overline{p(\omega)}.
\]
Using $(\theta)_{(q)}=(\theta)_q$, we obtain
\[
\bigl(\mathcal D_qH(0)\bigr)(p^*)
=(\theta)_q
\int_S f(\omega)\overline{p(\omega)}\,du(\omega),
\qquad p\in\mathcal P_{(q)}.
\]
The coefficient $(\theta)_q$ is nonzero by the assumption
$\theta\notin-\mathbb N_0$.

Let $E=\mathcal P_{(q)}|_S$, and let $f_E$ be the orthogonal
projection of $f$ onto $E$. By the uniqueness statement following
\eqref{12}, $E$ is the full $K$-isotypic component of its type.
The identity above shows that $\mathcal D_qH(0)\ne0$ implies
$f_E\ne0$. As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{56},
Lemma~\ref{29} and irreducibility of $E$ then give
$
P_{\sigma,\theta}E\subset\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega).
$
Lemma~\ref{16} therefore gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)
\in\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega)
\ \ 
\mbox{for every minimal tripotent}\ c.\]
By \eqref{47},
\[
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
=
\frac{(\theta)_q}{(\frac nr)_q}\,
t^q(1-t^2)^{j_0}
{}_2F_1(1,j_0;\sigma+1;t^2).
\]
Put $\rho=1-t^2$. If $\sigma\in\mathbb N$, then
$\frac nr\in\mathbb N$, and $\theta\notin-\mathbb N_0$
forces $\theta\in\mathbb N$. Thus
$\sigma-j_0=q-1+\theta\in\mathbb N$.
If $\sigma\notin\mathbb N$, then $\sigma-j_0$ is not an
integer, since $j_0\in\mathbb N$. Thus Lemma~\ref{551}
applies with $\lambda=\sigma$ and $\mu=\sigma-j_0$;
in particular, $\lambda-\mu=j_0>0$.
Using $t^q=(1-\rho)^{q/2}$ in the radial formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
={}&R(\rho)+\frac{(\theta)_q}{(\frac nr)_q}
(1-\rho)^{q/2-\sigma}
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{\Gamma(\sigma+1)\Gamma(j_0-\sigma)}
     {\Gamma(j_0)}\,\rho^\sigma,
&\sigma\notin\mathbb N,\\
\displaystyle
\frac{(-1)^{\sigma-j_0+1}\Gamma(\sigma+1)}
     {(\sigma-j_0)!\,\Gamma(j_0)}
     \,\rho^\sigma\log\rho,
&\sigma\in\mathbb N.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here $R$ is analytic near $\rho=0$, and the coefficient of the
singular term in each case is nonzero. Since
$(1-\rho)^{q/2-\sigma}$ is analytic and nonzero at $0$,
when $\sigma\notin\mathbb N$ the term
$\rho^\sigma(1-\rho)^{q/2-\sigma}$ does not belong to
$C^{\lfloor\sigma\rfloor,\varepsilon}$ for any
$\varepsilon>\sigma-\lfloor\sigma\rfloor$.
When $\sigma\in\mathbb N$, the term
$\rho^\sigma\log\rho\,(1-\rho)^{q/2-\sigma}$ is not $C^\sigma$.
Thus the radial function does not have the regularity required by
$\mathcal R^\sigma$.
This contradicts the regularity of
$P_{\sigma,\theta}(\ell_c^q)$. Therefore
$\mathcal D_qH(0)=0$.

For $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$, set
\[
F_{\widetilde g}
=P_{\sigma,\theta}\pi_{\sigma,\theta}(\widetilde g)f,
\qquad
H_{\widetilde g}
=h(z,z)^{-j_0}F_{\widetilde g}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{29} allows the same argument to be applied to
$F_{\widetilde g}$, so $\mathcal D_qH_{\widetilde g}(0)=0$.
Writing $g=\pi(\widetilde g)$, formula~\eqref{380} with
$L=q-1$ gives
\[
\mathcal D_qH_{\widetilde g}(0)
=
\overline{J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(0)}^{\,j_0/p_\Omega}
J_{\widetilde g^{-1}}(0)^{-(q-1)/p_\Omega}
B_g(0)(\mathcal D_qH)(g^{-1}0).
\]
The Jacobian factors are nonzero and $B_g(0)$ is invertible.
Thus $(\mathcal D_qH)(g^{-1}0)=0$ for every $g\in G$.
Transitivity of $G$ gives $\mathcal D_qH=0$ on $\Omega$,
which is \eqref{58}.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E$ denote the space on the left of \eqref{60}.
Both polynomial factors are $K$-invariant, hence so is $E$.
By Lemma~\ref{16} and
$\partial_j\ell_\xi^q=q\overline{\xi_j}\ell_\xi^{q-1}$,
\[
\mathcal P_{(q-1)}
=
\operatorname{span}\{\ell_\xi^{q-1}:\operatorname{rank}\xi=1\}
=
\operatorname{span}\{\partial_jp:
p\in\mathcal P_{(q)},\ 1\le j\le n\}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{21} and the definition \eqref{59} therefore give
\[
\Pi_HE=\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S,
\qquad
(I-\Pi_H)E=\mathcal M_q.
\]

Let $\tau$ be the $K$-type of $\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S$.
By the uniqueness statement following \eqref{12},
$\Pi_\tau^S$ is the orthogonal projection onto this space.
For $v\in E$, we have $\Pi_Hv\in\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S$
and $v-\Pi_Hv\perp H^2(S)$, so
$\Pi_\tau^Sv=\Pi_Hv$. Since $E$ is $K$-invariant,
the character formula gives $\Pi_\tau^SE\subset E$.
Thus $\Pi_HE\subset E$, and
\[
E=\Pi_HE\oplus(I-\Pi_H)E
 =\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S\oplus\mathcal M_q.
\]
The sum is orthogonal because $\Pi_H$ is an orthogonal
projection. Finally, $\Pi_H$ commutes with $K$, so
$\mathcal M_q=(I-\Pi_H)E$ is $K$-invariant.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $z,w$ near $0$, put
\[
\widetilde F(z,w)
=
h(z,w)^\sigma
\int_S
h(z,\omega)^{-\frac nr}
h(\omega,w)^{-\sigma}
f(\omega)\,du(\omega).
\]
Then $\widetilde F(z,z)=F(z)$. By \eqref{13} with $u=1$ and the
degree-one case of \eqref{14},
$$h(x,w)^{-1}=1+\sum_{k=1}^n x_k\bar w_k+O(|w|^2),\ \ 
\mbox{as}\ w\to0.$$ Since $h(x,0)=1$, differentiating the above formula gives
$$\bar\partial_{w_j}h(x,w)\big|_{w=0}=-x_j.$$
As $f\in L^2(S)\subset L^1(S)$, we may differentiate under the
integral near the origin and obtain
\[
\bar\partial_{w_j}\widetilde F(z,0)
=
\sigma\left[
\int_S h(z,\omega)^{-\frac nr}\omega_jf(\omega)\,du(\omega)
-z_j\int_S h(z,\omega)^{-\frac nr}f(\omega)\,du(\omega)
\right].
\]
For $p\in\mathcal P_{(q)}$, the Faraut--Kor\'anyi expansion and Fischer
adjointness give
\[
p^*(\partial_z)h(z,\omega)^{-\frac nr}\Big|_{z=0}
=
\left(\frac nr\right)_{(q)}\overline{p(\omega)}
\]
and
\[
p^*(\partial_z)
\left[z_jh(z,\omega)^{-\frac nr}\right]\Big|_{z=0}
=
\left(\frac nr\right)_{(q-1)}
\overline{\partial_jp(\omega)}.
\]
Since \(\left(\frac nr\right)_{(q)} = \sigma\left(\frac nr\right)_{(q-1)}\),
restriction to the diagonal gives \eqref{62}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{64}
For every $q\ge1$, the space $\mathcal M_q$ in \eqref{59} is
irreducible and is the full $K$-isotypic component of its type in
$L^2(S)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the function spaces below, their product means the span of all
pointwise products on $S$. Write $1^d$ for a tuple of $d$ ones,
with $1^0$ empty.

For tube-type domains, $S=K/K_1$ is a compact symmetric space;
see \cite[Section~1]{ZhangRec95}. Hence $L^2(S)$ contains at most
one copy of each irreducible $K$-type.

By \cite[Section~2, proof of Lemma~2]{ZhangRec95},
$\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S$ is one-dimensional. A nonzero element
of its conjugate is nowhere zero on $S$, since $K$ acts
transitively on $S$. Thus pointwise multiplication by this
element realizes
$\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
 \mathcal P_{(1^{r-1},0)}|_S$
as the product of an irreducible $K$-type with a
one-dimensional character, and this product is irreducible
\cite[Section~2.3]{FultonHarris}.

The one-dimensional $K$-type
$\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}$ has signature
$(-1,\ldots,-1)$. Hence
$\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(1^{r-1},0)}|_S$
has signature
$(1^{r-1},0)+(-1,\ldots,-1)=(0^{r-1},-1)$
by \cite[Lemma~3]{ZhangRec95}.
The $K$-type $\overline{\mathcal P_{(1)}|_S}$
has the same signature. Since $L^2(S)$ is multiplicity-free,
\[
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1)}|_S}
=
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(1^{r-1},0)}|_S.
\]

For the pointwise product of $\mathcal P_{(q)}|_S$ and
$\mathcal P_{(1^{r-1},0)}|_S$,
\cite[Theorem~1(1)]{ZhangRec95} allows only the two
$K$-types displayed below. The recurrence formula
\cite[Theorem~1(2)]{ZhangRec95} shows that the product
of the normalized $K_1$-fixed vectors of these two spaces
has a nonzero component in each type. Since the pointwise
product space is $K$-invariant, it contains both full types:
\[
\mathcal P_{(q)}|_S\,
\mathcal P_{(1^{r-1},0)}|_S
=
\mathcal P_{(q,1^{r-1})}|_S
\oplus
\mathcal P_{(q+1,1^{r-2},0)}|_S.
\]
Multiplying by $\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}$
and using the preceding equality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal P_{(q)}|_S\,\overline{\mathcal P_{(1)}|_S}
&=
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(q,1^{r-1})}|_S\oplus
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(q+1,1^{r-2},0)}|_S\\
&=
\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S
\oplus
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(q+1,1^{r-2},0)}|_S.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last equality again follows from the signatures and
multiplicity one in $L^2(S)$. Comparing with \eqref{60},
we obtain
\[
\mathcal M_q
=
\overline{\mathcal P_{(1^r)}|_S}\,
\mathcal P_{(q+1,1^{r-2},0)}|_S.
\]
The right-hand side is irreducible, has signature
$(q,0^{r-2},-1)$, and is the full $K$-isotypic
component of that type in $L^2(S)$.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\ell_c^q\in\mathcal P_{(q)}$, summing the corresponding
generators in \eqref{59} with coefficients $c_j$ gives
$f_c\in\mathcal M_q$; here we use $\|c\|=1$ and
$\sigma=\frac nr+q-1$.

Put $x=t^2$ and first suppose $0<t<1$. Using
$t\overline{\ell_c}=1-(1-t\overline{\ell_c})$ in the
Poisson kernel \eqref{8}, together with \eqref{42}, gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\ell_c^q\overline{\ell_c})(tc)
=
\frac{1}{t}\left(
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
-
P_{\sigma,\frac nr-1}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
\right).
\]
Since $\sigma=\frac nr+q-1$, Lemma~\ref{43}, in the form
\eqref{47}, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\ell_c^q)(tc)=t^q,\ \ 
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\ell_c^{q-1})(tc)=t^{q-1},\\
&P_{\sigma,\frac nr-1}(\ell_c^q)(tc)
=
\frac{\frac nr-1}{\sigma}\,
t^q(1-x)\,{}_2F_1(1,1;\sigma+1;x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, using $\sigma-q=\frac nr-1$,
\[
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f_c(tc)
=
\frac{\frac nr-1}{\sigma}\,t^{q-1}
\left[1-(1-x)\,{}_2F_1(1,1;\sigma+1;x)\right].
\]
Comparing coefficients in the Gauss series gives
\[
1-(1-x)\,{}_2F_1(1,1;\sigma+1;x)
=
\frac{\sigma x}{\sigma+1}\,
{}_2F_1(1,1;\sigma+2;x).
\]
This proves \eqref{66} for $t>0$, and continuity gives it at $t=0$.

Since $r>1$, we have
\(\frac nr=1+\frac a2(r-1)>1\).
Put $\rho=1-t^2$. Lemma~\ref{551}, with
$\lambda=\sigma+1$ and $\mu=\sigma$, gives
\[
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f_c(tc)
=
H(\rho)
+
\left(\frac nr-1\right)
(1-\rho)^{(q+1)/2-\sigma-1}
\begin{cases}
\Gamma(\sigma+1)\Gamma(-\sigma)\rho^\sigma,
&\sigma\notin\mathbb N,\\[2mm]
(-1)^{\sigma+1}\rho^\sigma\log\rho,
&\sigma\in\mathbb N,
\end{cases}
\]
where $H$ is analytic near $\rho=0$. The coefficient
of the singular term is nonzero in either case.
Therefore $P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f_c\notin
\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega)$ and the proof is complete.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma~\ref{64}, $\mathcal M_q$ is
irreducible and is the full $K$-isotypic component of its type.
Let $f_{\mathcal M}$ be the orthogonal projection of $f$
onto $\mathcal M_q$. By Lemma~\ref{29},
$P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f_{\mathcal M}
\in\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega)$.
As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{57}, irreducibility of
$\mathcal M_q$ implies that, if $f_{\mathcal M}\ne0$, then
\[
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}\mathcal M_q
\subset\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega).
\]
This contradicts Lemma~\ref{65}, since $f_c\in\mathcal M_q$.
Hence $f_{\mathcal M}=0$, or equivalently
$f\perp\mathcal M_q$.

By Lemma~\ref{61}, the orthogonality
$f\perp\mathcal M_q$ gives
$
\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF(0)=0.
$


Now let $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$ and put
$
F_{\widetilde g}
=
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}
\pi_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\widetilde g)f.
$
By Lemma~\ref{29},
$
F_{\widetilde g}\in\mathcal R^\sigma(\overline\Omega).
$
Applying the preceding argument to
$\pi_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\widetilde g)f$ gives
$
\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF_{\widetilde g}(0)=0.
$
Since this holds for every $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$ and
$
q=\sigma-\frac nr+1,
$
Lemma~\ref{35} gives \(\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF=0 \ \text{on }\Omega\).
This is \eqref{68}.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{73}
For every $f\in C(S)$,
\[
\lim_{t\uparrow1}
\sup_{\omega_0\in S}
\left|
P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f(t\omega_0)-f(\omega_0)
\right|=0.
\]
For every $f\in L^2(S)$, \(P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f(t\,\cdot)\longrightarrow f \quad\text{in }L^2(S)\)
as $t\uparrow1$. In particular, if $P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f$ extends
continuously to $\overline\Omega$, then $f$ has a continuous representative
and \(f=\left.P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f\right|_S\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write \(T_tf(\omega_0)=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f(t\omega_0)\).
We use the uniform boundary limit for the Poisson--Szeg\H{o}
transform \(P_{\frac nr,\frac nr}\) on $C(S)$, given by
\cite[Theorem~4.3]{BK07} at $s=n/r$, with the normalization
in \eqref{72}.

We first compare the kernels.  For $\omega_0,\omega\in S$, put
$p(\zeta)=h(\zeta\omega_0,\omega)$.  By \eqref{13} with $u=-1$,
$p$ is a polynomial of degree at most $r$, and $p(0)=1$.
The Szeg\H{o}-kernel formula \cite[(3.18)]{Koranyi} gives
$p(\zeta)\ne0$ for $|\zeta|<1$.  Thus
$p(\zeta)=\prod_{j=1}^{d}(1-\lambda_j\zeta)$, where $d\le r$
and $|\lambda_j|\le1$.  For $0\le t<1$ this gives
\[
|h(t\omega_0,\omega)|\ge(1-t)^r,
\qquad h(t\omega_0,t\omega_0)=(1-t^2)^r,
\]
the second identity following from \eqref{9}.  Since
$\sigma-\frac nr\in\mathbb N_0$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{501}
|\mathcal K_\sigma(t\omega_0,\omega)|
=
\left(\frac{h(t\omega_0,t\omega_0)}{|h(t\omega_0,\omega)|}\right)^{\sigma-\frac nr}
\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)
\le C\,\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega),
\qquad C=2^{r(\sigma-\frac nr)}.
\end{equation}

The positivity of $\mathcal K_{\frac nr}$, \eqref{72}, and
\eqref{501} give
\[
\|T_tf\|_\infty\le C\|f\|_\infty,
\qquad f\in C(S),\quad 0\le t<1.
\]
To prove convergence on a dense subspace of $C(S)$, fix $e_0\in S$
and put \(d_{e_0}(\omega)=\|\omega-e_0\|\).  By the cited
Poisson--Szeg\H{o} boundary limit,
\[
P_{\frac nr,\frac nr}d_{e_0}(te_0)
\longrightarrow d_{e_0}(e_0)=0.
\]
The $K$-invariance of the base kernel and $du$, and the transitive
unitary action of $K$ on $S$, show that
\[
\int_S\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)
\|\omega-\omega_0\|\,du(\omega)
=P_{\frac nr,\frac nr}d_{e_0}(te_0)
\]
for every $\omega_0\in S$.  If $f$ is Lipschitz on $S$ with
constant $L_f$, then
\eqref{72} and \eqref{501} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
|T_tf(\omega_0)-f(\omega_0)|
&\le C\int_S\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)
|f(\omega)-f(\omega_0)|\,du(\omega)\\
&\le CL_f
P_{\frac nr,\frac nr}d_{e_0}(te_0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $T_tf\to f$ uniformly for Lipschitz $f$.  These functions are
dense in $C(S)$; for $f\in C(S)$ and Lipschitz $g$,
\[
\|T_tf-f\|_\infty
\le(C+1)\|f-g\|_\infty+\|T_tg-g\|_\infty.
\]
The uniform bound on $T_t$ now gives $T_tf\to f$ uniformly for
every $f\in C(S)$.

By \eqref{72}, for every \(\omega_0\in S\),
\[
\int_S\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)\,du(\omega)=1.
\]
For fixed \(t\), $K$-invariance makes
\[
A_t(\omega):=
\int_S\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)\,du(\omega_0)
\]
constant on \(S\). Since \(du(S)=1\), Fubini's theorem and the
preceding identity give
\[
A_t(\omega)
=\int_S A_t(\eta)\,du(\eta)
=\int_S\int_S
  \mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\eta)
  \,du(\eta)\,du(\omega_0)
=1.
\]
By \eqref{501} and Cauchy--Schwarz with respect to the probability
measure \(\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)\,du(\omega)\),
\[
|T_tf(\omega_0)|^2
\le C^2\int_S\mathcal K_{\frac nr}(t\omega_0,\omega)
|f(\omega)|^2\,du(\omega).
\]
Integrating in \(\omega_0\) and using \(A_t(\omega)=1\) gives
\[
\|T_tf\|_{L^2(S)}\le C\|f\|_{L^2(S)},
\qquad 0\le t<1.
\]
For \(f\in L^2(S)\) and \(g\in C(S)\), it follows that
\[
\|T_tf-f\|_{L^2(S)}
\le (C+1)\|f-g\|_{L^2(S)}+\|T_tg-g\|_{L^2(S)}.
\]
The last term tends to zero by the uniform convergence proved above.
Since \(C(S)\) is dense in \(L^2(S)\), we obtain \(T_tf\to f\) in
\(L^2(S)\).

Finally, if \(F=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f\) is continuous on
\(\overline\Omega\), then \(F(t\,\cdot)\to F|_S\) uniformly, while
the result just proved gives \(F(t\,\cdot)\to f\) in \(L^2(S)\).
Hence \(f=F|_S\) almost everywhere.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $r=1$, we have $c=0$, and both identities are immediate.
Assume $r\ge2$. Write
\[
c=c_1+\cdots+c_{r-1},\qquad w=\rho c_r,\quad 0\le\rho<1,
\]
where $(c_1,\ldots,c_r)$ is a Jordan frame. When $w=0$, choose
$c_r$ arbitrarily in $V_0(c)$.

For the spaces $V_{ij}$ in \eqref{502},
\cite[formula~(23)]{EYZ} gives
\[
B(c+w,\overline{c+w})|_{V_{ij}}
=(1-|t_i|^2)(1-|t_j|^2)I|_{V_{ij}},
\quad
t_0=0,\quad t_1=\cdots=t_{r-1}=1,\quad t_r=\rho.
\]
The formula also holds when $t_i=1$, since both sides are polynomial
in the spectral coefficients.  By \eqref{503}, every summand of
$V_1(c)\oplus V_2(c)$ has an index among $1,\ldots,r-1$, so the
operator vanishes there.  Also by \eqref{503},
$V_0(c)=V_{rr}\oplus V_{0r}$, and the restrictions to these two
spaces are respectively $(1-\rho^2)^2I$ and $(1-\rho^2)I$.
These agree with the restrictions of $B_0(w,\bar w)$ in
\eqref{75}, proving \eqref{77}.

Since  \(c\) is
orthogonal to \(c_r\), and both are
tripotents, direct computations show that
\[
Q(c+w)\overline{(c+w)}
=Q(c+\rho c_r)\overline{(c+\rho c_r)}
=c+\rho^3c_r,
\qquad
Q(w)\bar w=\rho^3c_r.
\]
Subtracting gives \eqref{78} and the proof is complete.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{81}
If $f\in C(S)$ and
$
F=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}f \in C^{b+1+\sigma-\frac nr}(\overline\Omega).
$
Then
\[
\Pi_{H^{\sigma-\frac nr+1,1}(V_0(c))}
\bigl(f(c+\cdot)\bigr)=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the spherical-harmonic method of Graham and Chen--Li
\cite{Graham,ChenLi}.

Put $p=\sigma-\frac nr+1\in\mathbb N$ and
$m=b+p\in\mathbb N$. On $\partial\Omega_0(c)$, write
$g_c(u)=f(c+u)$. We show that its
$H^{p,1}(\mathbb C^{b+1})$ component vanishes.

For $0<t<1$ and $\zeta\in\partial\Omega_0(c)$, set
\[
U_c(t\zeta)
=
\Pi_{H^{p,1}}\bigl[F_c(t\,\cdot)\bigr](\zeta).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{73}, $F_c|_{\partial\Omega_0(c)}=g_c$.
Hence
\[
U_c|_{\partial\Omega_0(c)}
=
\Pi_{H^{p,1}(V_0(c))}g_c
=
\Pi_{H^{p,1}(V_0(c))}\bigl(f(c+\cdot)\bigr).
\] This projection is a
compact-group average and preserves the assumed $C^m$ regularity
on  $\overline{\Omega_0(c)}$. The operator in \eqref{80} commutes with the
$U(b+1)$-action; hence $U_c$ also satisfies \eqref{80}.



Choose homogeneous harmonic polynomials $(Y_\ell)$ whose restrictions
form an orthonormal basis of $H^{p,1}(\mathbb C^{b+1})$ on the unit
sphere. For $w\ne0$, we can write $U_c$ as
\[
\sum_\ell Y_\ell(w)\Phi_\ell(x),
\qquad x=\|w\|^2.
\]
For a harmonic polynomial $Y$ of bidegree $(p,1)$,
$\sum_jw_j\partial_jY=pY$ and
$\sum_j\bar w_j\bar\partial_jY=Y$. Using these identities and
$\sigma-\frac nr=p-1$ in \eqref{80}, then using the linear
independence of the $Y_\ell$ on each sphere, we find that each
$\Phi_\ell$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{83}
x(1-x)\Phi''+(m+2-3x)\Phi'-\Phi=0.
\end{equation}
This is Gauss's hypergeometric equation with parameters
$1,1$ and $m+2$.

Since the restrictions of the $Y_\ell$ are orthonormal, therefore
\[
t^{p+1}\Phi_\ell(t^2)
=
\int_{\partial\Omega_0(c)}
U_c(t\zeta)\overline{Y_\ell(\zeta)}\,d\zeta,
\qquad 0<t<1,
\]
where $d\zeta$ is normalized surface measure. Because
$U_c\in C^m(\overline{\Omega_0(c)})$, the integral is bounded
as $t\downarrow0$ and is $C^m$ up to $t=1$. The change of
variable $x=t^2$ is smooth and invertible near $t=1$.
Consequently,
\[
x^{(p+1)/2}\Phi_\ell(x)=O(1)\quad(x\downarrow0),
\qquad
\Phi_\ell\in C^m\text{ near }x=1.
\]

At $x=0$, equation~\eqref{83} has the regular solution
${}_2F_1(1,1;m+2;x)$. An independent solution has leading
order $x^{-m-1}$ and violates the first condition, since
$p+1<2(m+1)$. Hence
\[
\Phi_\ell(x)=a_\ell\,{}_2F_1(1,1;m+2;x).
\]
It follows that
\[
U_c(w)=Y(w)\,{}_2F_1(1,1;m+2;\|w\|^2)
\]
for a harmonic polynomial $Y$ of bidegree $(p,1)$.

Lemma~\ref{551}, with $\lambda=m+1$, $\mu=m$, and
$\rho=1-x$, gives
\[
{}_2F_1(1,1;m+2;x)
=A(1-x)+(-1)^{m+1}(m+1)x^{-m-1}
(1-x)^m\log(1-x),
\]
where $A$ is analytic near $0$. If $Y\ne0$, choose
$\zeta\in\partial\mathbb B^{b+1}$ with $Y(\zeta)\ne0$.
Along $w=t\zeta$, the factor $Y(t\zeta)=t^{p+1}Y(\zeta)$
is smooth and nonzero near $t=1$, whereas
$(1-t^2)^m\log(1-t^2)$ is not $C^m$ there. This contradicts
the $C^m$ regularity of $U_c$. Hence $U_c=0$. Its boundary value is the
$H^{p,1}(\mathbb C^{b+1})$ component of $g_c$,
so this component vanishes.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{84}
Let $q\ge1$ and $f\in C(S)$.  Suppose that, for every tripotent $c$ of
rank $r-1$, \(\Pi_{H^{q,1}(V_0(c))} \bigl[w\mapsto f(c+w)\bigr]=0\).
Then \(f\perp\mathcal M_q\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $r=1$, then $\Omega$ is the unit ball of $V$,
and $0$ is the only tripotent of rank $r-1$. By \eqref{10},
$\mathcal P_{(q)}$ is the full space of holomorphic homogeneous
polynomials of degree $q$. Thus the left-hand side of \eqref{60}
is the restriction to $S$ of all polynomials of bidegree $(q,1)$.
The decomposition of bihomogeneous polynomials in
\cite[Section~2.2, Lemma~3]{BSW}, restricted to the unit sphere, gives
\[
\operatorname{span}\{(p\bar\ell)|_S:
p\in\mathcal P_{(q)},\ \ell\in\mathcal P_{(1)}\}
=H^{q,1}(V)\oplus\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S,
\]
with orthogonal summands. Comparing this with \eqref{60} gives
$\mathcal M_q=H^{q,1}(V)$.
The hypothesis is then $\Pi_{H^{q,1}(V)}f=0$, so
$f\perp\mathcal M_q$.

The case $r>1$ is proved in Appendix~\ref{90}.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $q=\sigma-\frac nr+1$. By Lemma~\ref{73}, $f$ has the
continuous representative $F|_S$. Lemma~\ref{81} gives
\(\Pi_{H^{q,1}(V_0(c))}[w\mapsto f(c+w)]=0\)
for every tripotent $c$ of rank $r-1$. Proposition~\ref{84}
therefore yields $f\perp\mathcal M_q$, and Lemma~\ref{61} gives
\(\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF(0)=0\).

For $\widetilde g\in\widetilde G$, put
\(F_{\widetilde g}=P_{\sigma,\frac nr}
\pi_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\widetilde g)f\).
By Lemma~\ref{29}, $F_{\widetilde g}$ has the same boundary
regularity as $F$. Applying the preceding argument to the
boundary datum $\pi_{\sigma,\frac nr}(\widetilde g)f$ gives
\(\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF_{\widetilde g}(0)=0\).
Lemma~\ref{35} now transfers these identities at the origin
to every point of $\Omega$. Hence
$\bar\partial\mathcal D_qF=0$ on $\Omega$, which is \eqref{71}.

title: Proof
body_md:
In the scalar realization, $F=P_{\sigma,\theta}f$, where
$\sigma=\frac nr-\frac{s+\nu}{2}$ and
$\theta=\frac nr-\frac{s-\nu}{2}$. The first and second rows
follow from Proposition~\ref{54} and Theorem~\ref{56}, respectively.

In the third row, $s=\nu\in-\mathbb N_0$ and
$\mathbb D_{-\nu,0}F=\mathcal D_{1-\nu}F$ in the
Harish--Chandra trivialization by \eqref{36}. Theorems~\ref{67}
and~\ref{70} give $\bar\partial\mathcal D_{1-\nu}F=0$ in
the tube and non-tube cases, respectively. Since the Dolbeault
operator acts componentwise in this trivialization, this is the
equation in the third row.

In the fourth row, set $m=\sigma\in\mathbb N$ and
$q=-\theta\in\mathbb N_0$. By \eqref{36},
\[
\mathbb D_{q,m}F
=h(z,z)^m\mathcal D_{q+1}\bigl(h(z,z)^{-m}F\bigr).
\]
Thus Proposition~\ref{54} gives the fourth row.

In the fifth row, set $L=\sigma-\frac nr\in\mathbb N_0$
and $j=\frac nr-\theta\in\mathbb N$. The condition
$\theta\notin-\mathbb N_0$ allows us to apply
Theorem~\ref{57}. Since \eqref{36} gives
\[
\mathbb D_{L,j}F
=h(z,z)^j\mathcal D_{L+1}\bigl(h(z,z)^{-j}F\bigr),
\]
that theorem yields the fifth row.

The parameter sets in \eqref{52} are exactly the union of
these five rows. The final row therefore follows from
Proposition~\ref{51}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{386}--\eqref{387}, $\Delta_\Omega$ is a positive
constant multiple of the Laplace--Beltrami operator of the
Bergman metric. The assumed boundary regularity gives
$F\in C(\overline\Omega)$, so Inoue's Poisson representation
\cite[Theorem, pp.~532--533]{Inoue} applies.

By \eqref{151}, its Poisson--Szeg\H{o} kernel is
\[
\frac{|C(z,\omega)|^2}{C(z,z)}
=
\frac{h(z,z)^{n/r}}{|h(z,\omega)|^{2n/r}}.
\]
Both representations use the normalized $K$-invariant probability
measure $du$ on $S$.
Hence $F=P_{n/r,n/r}(F|_S)$ by \eqref{8}, with
$F|_S\in C(S)\subset L^2(S)$. This is the scalar form of
$P_{0,0}$. The third row of Theorem~\ref{3} and \eqref{36}
therefore give $\bar\partial\mathcal D_1F=0$.

Since $\mathcal P_{(1)}$ consists of linear holomorphic
polynomials, the coordinates of $\mathcal D_1F$  are
$(\partial_1F,\ldots,\partial_nF)$. Thus
$\bar\partial_j\partial_iF=0$ for all $i,j$, so $F$ is
pluriharmonic.

title: Definition
body_md:
For $s\in S$, let $\mathcal I_s$ be the set of minimal tripotents
$e\in V$ for which $s-e$ is a rank-$(r-1)$ tripotent orthogonal to $e$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $K$ preserves the rank and orthogonality of tripotents, therefore for $k\in K$ and $(s,e)\in X$, \(k\cdot(s,e):=(ks,ke)\in X\) and then the group $K$ acts on $X$.
Given $(s,e)\in X$,
choose $k_1\in K$ with $k_1s_0=s$. Then $k_1e_0\in\mathcal I_s$.
Since $K_s$ acts transitively on $\mathcal I_s$, there is
$k_2\in K_s$ such that $k_2k_1e_0=e$. Hence
$(s,e)=(k_2k_1s_0,k_2k_1e_0)$ and therefore the action of $K$ on $X$ is transitive. 

For each $\omega\in\partial\Omega_0(c_0)$, the pair
$(c_0+\omega,\omega)$ belongs to $X$. Since $K$ acts transitively
on $X$, right invariance of Haar measure gives
\[
\int_K F\bigl(k(c_0+\omega),k\omega\bigr)\,dk
=
\int_K F(ks_0,ke_0)\,dk.
\]
Integrating over $\omega$ proves the equality of the first two
integrals in \eqref{94}.

By \eqref{92}, $\mu_{ks_0}=k_*\mu_{s_0}$ for $k\in K$.
Also, $du$ is the image of normalized Haar measure under
$k\mapsto ks_0$. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_S\int_{\mathcal I_s}F(s,e)\,d\mu_s(e)\,du(s)
&=\int_K\int_{K_{s_0}}F(ks_0,khe_0)\,dh\,dk\\
&=\int_{K_{s_0}}\int_K F(khs_0,khe_0)\,dk\,dh=\int_K F(ks_0,ke_0)\,dk.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses $hs_0=s_0$; the last uses right
invariance of Haar measure on $K$. This proves \eqref{94}.

title: Definition
body_md:
For a tripotent $c$ of rank $r-1$, define \(R_c:C(S)\longrightarrow H^{q,1}(V_0(c))\)
by \[R_ch = \Pi_{H^{q,1}(V_0(c))} \bigl[w\mapsto h(c+w)\bigr],\ \ h\in C(S).\]
For $P\in\mathcal E_q$, define
\begin{equation}\label{95}
(\mathcal A_qP)(s)
=
\int_{\mathcal I_s}
(R_{s-e}(P|_S))(e)\,d\mu_s(e),
\qquad
s\in S.
\end{equation}

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\operatorname{rank}c=r-1$, therefore $\dim_{\mathbb C}W=b+1$. Choose orthonormal
coordinates on $W$ and write
$\Delta_W=\sum_{j=1}^{b+1}\partial_{w_j}\bar\partial_{w_j}$.
For a holomorphic homogeneous polynomial $p$ of degree $q$
and $u\in W$, direct differentiation gives
\[
\Delta_W(p\overline{\ell_u})=\partial_up,
\qquad
\Delta_W(\|w\|^2\partial_up)=(b+q)\partial_up.
\]
These identities show that
\(p\overline{\ell_u}
-\frac{\|w\|^2}{b+q}\partial_up\)
is harmonic and of bidegree $(q,1)$. Its restriction to
$\partial\Omega_0(c)$ therefore lies in $H^{q,1}(W)$.
Since  $\|w\|=1$ on $\partial \Omega_0(c)$ and 
$\partial_up|_{\partial \Omega_0(c)}\in H^{q-1,0}(W)$, and $ H^{q-1,0}(W)$ is orthogonal to
$H^{q,1}(W)$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{100}
\Pi_{H^{q,1}(W)}\bigl(p\overline{\ell_u}\bigr)
=
p\overline{\ell_u}|_S
-\frac1{b+q}\partial_up|_S
\qquad\text{on }\partial\Omega_0(c).
\end{equation}

Now consider \[w\longmapsto \ell_\xi(c+w)^q\overline{\ell_v(c+w)}, \quad w\in W.\]
Its term of bidegree $(q,1)$ is
$
\ell_\xi(w)^q\overline{\ell_v(w)}.
$
All the other terms have total degree at most $q$, their spherical
harmonic components therefore have degree at most $q$ and are
orthogonal to $H^{q,1}(W)$. Then
\[\Pi_{H^{q,1}(W)}\bigl[w\longmapsto \ell_\xi(c+w)^q\overline{\ell_v(c+w)}]=\Pi_{H^{q,1}(W)}(\ell_\xi^q\overline{\ell_v}).\]
Apply \eqref{100} to \(p(w)=\ell_\xi(w)^q\) and \( u=\operatorname{pr}_Wv\) and $\ell_v(w)=\ell_{\operatorname{pr}_Wv}(w)$ gives \eqref{98}.

It remains to evaluate \eqref{98} at $e$. Complete $e$ to a Jordan
frame $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ such that \[e_r=e, \quad c=e_1+\cdots+e_{r-1}, \quad s=e_1+\cdots+e_r.\]
Applying \eqref{503} to $c$ and $s$, with $V_{ij}$ as in
\eqref{502}, gives
\[W=V_{rr}\oplus V_{0r}=\mathbb Ce\oplus V_{0r}\ \mbox{and}\
V_1(s)=\bigoplus_{j=1}^rV_{0j}.\]
Since $D(e,\bar s)$ is the identity on $V_{0r}$ and is zero on
$V_{0j}$ for $j<r$, one has \[\operatorname{pr}_Wv = \overline{\ell_v(e)}\,e + D(e,\bar s)\operatorname{pr}_1(s)v.\]
Also, \(\partial_e\ell_\xi^q(e) = q\ell_\xi(e)^q\).
Therefore
\[
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_Wv}\ell_\xi^q(e)
=
q\ell_\xi(e)^q\overline{\ell_v(e)}
+
\partial_{D(e,\bar s)\operatorname{pr}_1(s)v}
\ell_\xi^q(e).
\]
Substituting this into \eqref{98} at $w=e$ gives \eqref{99}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{1000}
For $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and $y\in V$, the Fischer kernels satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{1001}
\left(\frac a2+m\right)
\bar\partial_y^wK^F_{(m+1)}(z,w)
=
\frac a2\ell_y(z)K^F_{(m)}(z,w)
+
\partial_{Q(z)\bar y}^zK^F_{(m)}(z,w).
\end{equation}
If $\xi\in V$ has rank one, then
\begin{equation}\label{1002}
\frac a2\ell_y(z)\ell_\xi(z)^m
+
\partial_{Q(z)\bar y}\ell_\xi^m(z)
=
m!\left(\frac a2+m\right)
\bar\partial_y^wK^F_{(m+1)}(z,w)\big|_{w=\xi}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the polynomial on the left of \eqref{1002} belongs to
$\mathcal P_{(m+1)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $z,w$ near $0$, recall that
\(z^{\bar w}=B(z,\bar w)^{-1}(z-Q(z)\bar w)\) is the quasi-inverse.
The symmetry principle gives \(z^{\bar w}=z+Q(z)\overline{w^{\bar z}}\).
The logarithmic derivative formulas for the generic norm
\cite[formulas~(1.13)--(1.14)]{WYZR} give
\[
\bar\partial_y^w h(z,w)^{-a/2}
=
\frac a2h(z,w)^{-a/2}\langle z^{\bar w},y\rangle,
\qquad
\partial_u^z h(z,w)^{-a/2}
=
\frac a2h(z,w)^{-a/2}\langle u,w^{\bar z}\rangle.
\]
By the outer symmetry of the Jordan triple product and the adjoint
relation for the trace form
\cite[Section~2.4, Theorem~2.2 (JT2) and formulas~(7)--(8)]{Clerc},
\begin{equation}\label{106}
\begin{aligned}
\langle Q(z)\bar u,y\rangle
&=
\frac12\langle D(z,\bar u)z,y\rangle
=
\frac12\langle z,D(u,\bar z)y\rangle
=
\frac12\langle z,D(y,\bar z)u\rangle
\\
&=
\frac12\langle D(z,\bar y)z,u\rangle
=
\langle Q(z)\bar y,u\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Hence
\[
\bar\partial_y^w h(z,w)^{-a/2}
=
\frac a2\ell_y(z)h(z,w)^{-a/2}
+
\partial_{Q(z)\bar y}^z h(z,w)^{-a/2}.
\]
At the parameter $a/2$, \eqref{13} becomes
\[h(z,w)^{-a/2}=\sum_{j\ge0}(a/2)_jK^F_{(j)}(z,w).\]
Comparing the terms of degree $m+1$ in $z$ and degree $m$ in
$\bar w$ proves \eqref{1001} near $(0,0)$, and hence everywhere
because both sides are polynomials. Setting $w=\xi$ and using
Lemma~\ref{16} (and $K^F_{(0)}=1$ when $m=0$) gives \eqref{1002}.
As a function of $z$, the right-hand side of \eqref{1002} lies in
$\mathcal P_{(m+1)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $m=0$, \eqref{102} follows from the normalization of $\mu_s$.
To prove \eqref{102} for $m\ge1$, fix $e_0\in\mathcal I_s$. By \eqref{92}, one has, for $k\in K$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathcal I_s}(k\cdot p)(e)\,d\mu_s(e)
=
\int_{K_s}p(k^{-1}he_0)\,dh
=
\int_{K_{k^{-1}s}}
p(hk^{-1}e_0)\,dh
=
\int_{\mathcal I_{k^{-1}s}}
p(e)\,d\mu_{k^{-1}s}(e).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here we used \(K_{k^{-1}s}=k^{-1}K_sk\)
and the invariance of normalized Haar measure under conjugation.

By \eqref{12} and Frobenius reciprocity, the $K$-type
$\mathcal P_{(m)}$ occurs with multiplicity one in $L^2(S)$.
The restriction map
$
p\longmapsto p|_S
$
is a nonzero $K$-equivariant map from $\mathcal P_{(m)}$ into
$L^2(S)$. We have just shown that
$
p\longmapsto
\left[
s\longmapsto
\int_{\mathcal I_s}p(e)\,d\mu_s(e)
\right]
$
is another $K$-equivariant map from $\mathcal P_{(m)}$ into
$L^2(S)$. By multiplicity one, there is a constant $c_m$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{105}
\int_{\mathcal I_s}p(e)\,d\mu_s(e)
=
c_mp(s),
\qquad
p\in\mathcal P_{(m)},\ s\in S.
\end{equation}

Take \(p=K^F_{(m)}(\,\cdot\,,s)\).
If $e\in\mathcal I_s$, then $s-e$ is orthogonal to $e$, and hence
$
\langle e,s\rangle=1.
$
By the Hermitian symmetry of $K^F_{(m)}$ and Lemma~\ref{16}, one has
 \[\int_{\mathcal I_s} K^F_{(m)}(e,s)\,d\mu_s(e) =\int_{\mathcal I_s} \overline{K^F_{(m)}(s,e)}\,d\mu_s(e)=\int_{\mathcal I_s} \frac1{m!}\,d\mu_s(e)= \frac1{m!}.\]

On the other hand, for $0<t<1$, \(h(\lambda s,ts)^{-a/2} = (1-\lambda t)^{-ar/2}\).
Since only one-row terms occur in \eqref{13} at the parameter $a/2$,
comparison of the coefficients of $(\lambda t)^m$ gives \[K^F_{(m)}(s,s) = \frac{(ar/2)_m}{(a/2)_m\,m!}.\]
Substituting these two values into \eqref{105} gives \(c_m = \frac{(a/2)_m}{(ar/2)_m}\).
This proves \eqref{102}.

We next prove \eqref{103}. For $m\ge1$, Lemma~\ref{16} reduces
this to $p=\ell_\xi^m$ with $\xi$ of rank one. For $m=0$, it suffices
to take $p=1=\ell_\xi^0$. Put $y=Q(s)\bar v$. By Lemma~\ref{1000},
the polynomial on the left of \eqref{1002} belongs to
$\mathcal P_{(m+1)}$.

Now let $e\in\mathcal I_s$.
For a maximal tripotent $s$, the Peirce rules for $Q(s)$ give \[Q(s)\overline{Q(s)\bar v}=\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v.\]
Moreover $e\in V_2(s)$ and $Q(s)\bar e=e$.  Using the adjoint relation
for $Q(s)$, or equivalently \eqref{106}, we therefore obtain
\[
\ell_y(e)=\overline{\ell_v(e)},
\qquad
\ell_y(s)=\overline{\ell_v(s)},
\qquad
Q(s)\bar y=\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v.
\]
See also \cite[Section~5.3]{Clerc}.
Since $e$ is minimal, one has $$Q(e)\bar{y}\in V_2(e) ,\  V_2(e)=\mathbb{C}e \ \mbox{and}\ Q(e)\bar{e}=e,$$ hence by  \eqref{106},  \(Q(e)\bar y=\ell_y(e)e\).
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial_{Q(e)\bar y}\ell_\xi^m(e)
&=
\ell_y(e)\partial_e\ell_\xi^m(e)=
m\ell_\xi(e)^m\overline{\ell_v(e)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The polynomial on the left of \eqref{1002} therefore takes the value
\(\left(\frac a2+m\right)\ell_\xi(e)^m\overline{\ell_v(e)}\)
at $e$. At $s$, its value is
\[
\frac a2
\ell_\xi(s)^m\overline{\ell_v(s)}
+
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v}\ell_\xi^m(s).
\]
Applying \eqref{102} in degree $m+1$ to this polynomial gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac a2+m\right)
\int_{\mathcal I_s}
\ell_\xi(e)^m\overline{\ell_v(e)}\,d\mu_s(e)
={}&
\frac{(a/2)_{m+1}}{(ar/2)_{m+1}}
\left[
\frac a2
\ell_\xi(s)^m\overline{\ell_v(s)}
+
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v}\ell_\xi^m(s)
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Dividing by $a/2+m$ gives
\[
\int_{\mathcal I_s}
\ell_\xi(e)^m\overline{\ell_v(e)}\,d\mu_s(e)
=
\frac{(a/2)_m}{(ar/2)_{m+1}}
\left[
\frac a2
\ell_\xi(s)^m\overline{\ell_v(s)}
+
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v}\ell_\xi^m(s)
\right].
\]
For $m\ge1$, the rank-one powers $\ell_\xi^m$ span
$\mathcal P_{(m)}$ by Lemma~\ref{16}; for $m=0$, they span the constants.
Hence \eqref{103} follows by linearity.

Finally, the Harish--Chandra decomposition
\(\mathfrak g_{\mathbb C}=V\oplus\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}\oplus\bar V\)
and the bracket relation \([x,\bar y]=D(x,\bar y)\) in
\cite[Section~2, formulas~(1)--(2)]{KZ} show that
\(D(x,\bar s)\in\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}\).
Since $\mathcal P_{(m)}$ is $K$-invariant, it is also invariant under
the derived action of $\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}$. More explicitly, if $A\in\mathfrak k$, then \(p(e^{tA}z)\in\mathcal P_{(m)}\)
for every $t$, and differentiation at $t=0$ gives \(z\longmapsto\partial_{Az}p(z)\in\mathcal P_{(m)}\).
By complex linearity, the same conclusion holds for
$A\in\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}$. Hence \(z\longmapsto \partial_{D(x,\bar s)z}p(z) \in\mathcal P_{(m)}\).

By the outer symmetry of the Jordan triple product, \[D(x,\bar s)s = D(s,\bar s)x = x.\]
We may therefore apply \eqref{102} to the polynomial \(z\longmapsto \partial_{D(x,\bar s)z}p(z)\).
This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathcal I_s}
\partial_{D(e,\bar s)x}p(e)\,d\mu_s(e)
&=
\int_{\mathcal I_s}
\partial_{D(x,\bar s)e}p(e)\,d\mu_s(e)=
\frac{(a/2)_m}{(ar/2)_m}
\partial_{D(x,\bar s)s}p(s)=
\frac{(a/2)_m}{(ar/2)_m}
\partial_xp(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves \eqref{104}.

title: Proof
body_md:
To see that $\mathsf T$ maps $\mathcal E_q$ into itself, let \[U(z)=\sum_{j=1}^np_j(z)\bar z_j, \quad p_j\in\mathcal P_{(q)}.\]
Since
$
\bar z=\sum_{l=1}^n\bar z_l\bar v_l,
$
the outer symmetry gives
\[
D(z,\bar z)v_j
=
\sum_{l=1}^n
\bar z_lD(z,\bar v_l)v_j
=
\sum_{l=1}^n
\bar z_lD(v_j,\bar v_l)z.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n
\partial_{D(z,\bar z)v_j}p_j(z)
=
\sum_{l=1}^n
\left(
\sum_{j=1}^n
\partial_{D(v_j,\bar v_l)z}p_j(z)
\right)\bar z_l.
\]
The proof of Lemma~\ref{101} shows that \(z\longmapsto \partial_{D(v_j,\bar v_l)z}p_j(z)\)
belongs to $\mathcal P_{(q)}$. Therefore the coefficient of each
$\bar z_l$ in the preceding expression belongs to
$\mathcal P_{(q)}$, and hence \[\sum_{j=1}^n \partial_{D(z,\bar z)v_j}p_j(z) \in\mathcal E_q.\]
Thus $\mathsf T\mathcal E_q\subset\mathcal E_q$.

It remains to prove invertibility.  Since $K$ acts unitarily on $V$,
$\mathfrak k$ consists of skew-Hermitian endomorphisms.  Moreover,
$D(z,\bar z)\in\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}$ and
$D(z,\bar z)^*=D(z,\bar z)$.  Writing
$\mathfrak k_{\mathbb C}=\mathfrak k\oplus i\mathfrak k$ as real vector
spaces, the Hermitian condition therefore gives \(D(z,\bar z)\in i\mathfrak k\).

Let $\mathcal B$ be the positive multiple of the complexified Killing form
for which \[\mathcal B(u,\bar v)=\langle u,v\rangle, \quad u,v\in V.\]
Its restriction to the real space $i\mathfrak k$ is positive definite.
Choose a $\mathcal B$-orthonormal basis $(Z_\gamma)$ of $i\mathfrak k$.
Then every $Z_\gamma$ acts Hermitianly on $V$.  Using \([z,\bar w]=D(z,\bar w)\)
and the invariance of $\mathcal B$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B(D(z,\bar z),Z_\gamma)
&=
\mathcal B([z,\bar z],Z_\gamma)
=
\mathcal B([Z_\gamma,z],\bar z)
=
\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{107a}
D(z,\bar z)
=
\sum_\gamma
\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle Z_\gamma.
\end{equation}

For fixed $\gamma$, define
\[
\mathsf C_\gamma U
=
\sum_{j=1}^n
\partial_{Z_\gamma v_j}p_j,
\qquad
U=\sum_{j=1}^np_j\bar z_j.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{16}, \(\mathsf C_\gamma U\in\mathcal P_{(q-1)}\).
If \(Z_\gamma v_j = \sum_l c^\gamma_{lj}v_l\),
then, because $Z_\gamma$ is Hermitian, \(c^\gamma_{jl}=\overline{c^\gamma_{lj}}\).
For $h\in\mathcal P_{(q-1)}$, Fischer adjointness in the two variables gives
\begin{equation}\label{107b}
\left\langle
\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle h,
U
\right\rangle_F
=
\langle h,\mathsf C_\gamma U\rangle_F.
\end{equation}
Indeed, \(\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle = \sum_{l,j}c^\gamma_{lj}z_j\bar z_l\),
so the left-hand side of \eqref{107b} is \(\sum_{l,j}c^\gamma_{lj} \langle h,\partial_jp_l\rangle_F\).
On the other hand, after interchanging $j$ and $l$,
\[
\mathsf C_\gamma U
=
\sum_{l,j}c^\gamma_{jl}\partial_jp_l
=
\sum_{l,j}\overline{c^\gamma_{lj}}\partial_jp_l.
\]
Since the Fischer inner product is conjugate-linear in its second variable,
this gives exactly \eqref{107b}.
Notice that we only use the pairing identity \eqref{107b}; no assertion is
needed that multiplication by $\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle$ preserves
$\mathcal E_q$.

By \eqref{107a},
\[
\sum_{j=1}^n
\partial_{D(z,\bar z)v_j}p_j
=
\sum_\gamma
\langle Z_\gamma z,z\rangle
\mathsf C_\gamma U.
\]
Taking the Fischer inner product with $U$ and applying \eqref{107b} with
$h=\mathsf C_\gamma U$ gives
\[
\left\langle
\sum_{j=1}^n
\partial_{D(z,\bar z)v_j}p_j,
U
\right\rangle_F
=
\sum_\gamma
\|\mathsf C_\gamma U\|_F^2.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{108}
\langle\mathsf TU,U\rangle_F
=
\frac{ab}{2}\|U\|_F^2
+
\left(b+\frac{ar}{2}+q\right)
\sum_\gamma
\|\mathsf C_\gamma U\|_F^2.
\end{equation}
Since $a>0$ and $b>0$, the right-hand side is positive whenever
$U\ne0$.  Thus $\mathsf T$ is injective.  Since $\mathcal E_q$ is
finite-dimensional, $\mathsf T$ is invertible.

\label{109}
For $\mathcal A_q$ defined in \eqref{95}, \(\operatorname{Ran}\mathcal A_q = \mathcal M_q\).

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider \(U = \ell_\xi^q\overline{\ell_v}\), where
\(\xi,v\in V\) and \(\operatorname{rank}\xi=1\).
By \eqref{99}, \eqref{103}, and \eqref{104}, with \(x=\operatorname{pr}_1(s)v\),
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathcal A_qU)(s)
=
\frac{(a/2)_q}{(b+q)(ar/2)_{q+1}}
\Bigg\{
b\left[
\frac a2\ell_\xi(s)^q\overline{\ell_v(s)}
+
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_2(s)v}\ell_\xi^q(s)
\right]
-
\left(\frac{ar}{2}+q\right)
\partial_{\operatorname{pr}_1(s)v}\ell_\xi^q(s)
\Bigg\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $s$ is maximal, \[V = V_2(s)\oplus V_1(s),\ 
\mbox{and}\ D(s,\bar s) = 2\operatorname{pr}_2(s) + \operatorname{pr}_1(s).\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{pr}_2(s)
=
D(s,\bar s)-I,
\qquad
\operatorname{pr}_1(s)
=
2I-D(s,\bar s),
\]
and hence
\begin{align}
(\mathcal A_qU)(s)
={}&
\frac{(a/2)_q}{(b+q)(ar/2)_{q+1}}
\Bigg[
\frac{ab}{2}
\ell_\xi(s)^q\overline{\ell_v(s)}
+
\left(b+\frac{ar}{2}+q\right)
\partial_{D(s,\bar s)v}\ell_\xi^q(s)
\notag\\
&\hspace{40mm}
-
(b+ar+2q)\partial_v\ell_\xi^q(s)
\Bigg].
\label{110}
\end{align}

Write \(v=\sum_{j=1}^n a_jv_j, \quad a_j=\langle v,v_j\rangle\).
Then \(\overline{\ell_v(z)} = \sum_{j=1}^n a_j\bar z_j\).
By the definition of $\mathsf T$, the first two terms in the brackets
in \eqref{110} are $(\mathsf TU)(s)$. Also, \[\partial_v\ell_\xi^q = q\langle v,\xi\rangle\ell_\xi^{q-1} \in \mathcal P_{(q-1)}.\]
Thus
\[
\mathcal A_qU
-
\frac{(a/2)_q}{(b+q)(ar/2)_{q+1}}
(\mathsf TU)|_S
\in
\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{16},
$\mathcal P_{(q)}$ is spanned by the polynomials
$\ell_\xi^q$ with $\operatorname{rank}\xi=1$. Hence
\[
\mathcal E_q
=
\operatorname{span}
\left\{
\ell_\xi^q\overline{\ell_v}:
\xi,v\in V,\ \operatorname{rank}\xi=1
\right\}.
\]
It follows by linearity that
\begin{equation}\label{111}
\mathcal A_qU
-
\frac{(a/2)_q}{(b+q)(ar/2)_{q+1}}
(\mathsf TU)|_S
\in
\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S,
\qquad
U\in\mathcal E_q.
\end{equation}

We next record a formula for the pairing with $\mathcal A_qU$.
For $g\in C(S)$ and $U\in\mathcal E_q$,
\begin{equation}\label{112}
\langle g,\mathcal A_qU\rangle_S
=
\int_K
\left\langle
R_{kc_0}g,
R_{kc_0}(U|_S)
\right\rangle
\,dk.
\end{equation}
To prove this, first suppose that \(U=\ell_\xi^q\overline{\ell_v}\) with\( \operatorname{rank}\xi=1\).
By \eqref{99} and \(\operatorname{pr}_1(s)=2I-D(s,\bar s)\),
the function \((s,e) \longmapsto (R_{s-e}(U|_S))(e)\)
is continuous on $X$. The same is therefore true for every
$U\in\mathcal E_q$ by linearity. Hence \eqref{95} and \eqref{94} give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle g,\mathcal A_qU\rangle_S
=
\int_K\int_{\partial\Omega_0(c_0)}
&g\bigl(k(c_0+\omega)\bigr)
\overline{(R_{kc_0}(U|_S))(k\omega)}
\,d\omega\,dk.
\end{aligned}
\]
For fixed $k\in K$, the map \(\omega\longmapsto k\omega\)
carries the normalized sphere measure on
$\partial\Omega_0(c_0)$ onto that on
$\partial\Omega_0(kc_0)$. Thus the inner integral is
\[
\int_{\partial\Omega_0(kc_0)}
g(kc_0+e)
\overline{(R_{kc_0}(U|_S))(e)}
\,de.
\]
Since $R_{kc_0}$ is the orthogonal projection onto
$H^{q,1}(V_0(kc_0))$, this is \(\left\langle R_{kc_0}g, R_{kc_0}(U|_S) \right\rangle\).
This proves \eqref{112}.

We now show that
\begin{equation}\label{113}
\mathcal A_qU
\perp
\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S,
\qquad
U\in\mathcal E_q.
\end{equation}
Let $h\in\mathcal P_{(q-1)}$. For every tripotent $c$ of rank $r-1$,
the function \(e\longmapsto h(c+e)\)
is a holomorphic polynomial of degree at most $q-1$ on $V_0(c)$.
Its homogeneous components belong to \(H^{m,0}(V_0(c)), \quad 0\le m\le q-1\),
and are orthogonal on the sphere to
$H^{q,1}(V_0(c))$. Hence \(R_ch=0\).
Applying \eqref{112} with $g=h$ gives \(\langle h,\mathcal A_qU\rangle_S=0\),
and \eqref{113} follows.

Since $\mathsf TU\in\mathcal E_q$, \eqref{111} and \eqref{91} imply \(\mathcal A_qU\in\mathcal E_q|_S\).
Now \eqref{91} and \eqref{113} give \(\mathcal A_qU\in\mathcal M_q\).

By Lemma~\ref{21}, the restriction of $\Pi_H$ to
$\mathcal E_q|_S$ is the orthogonal projection onto
$\mathcal P_{(q-1)}|_S$. Taking the $\mathcal M_q$ component in
\eqref{111}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{114}
\mathcal A_qU
=
\frac{(a/2)_q}{(b+q)(ar/2)_{q+1}}
(I-\Pi_H)\bigl((\mathsf TU)|_S\bigr).
\end{equation}
The scalar in \eqref{114} is nonzero. Since $\mathsf T$ is invertible, \(\mathsf T(\mathcal E_q) = \mathcal E_q\).
Therefore \eqref{91} and \eqref{114} give \(\operatorname{Ran}\mathcal A_q = (I-\Pi_H)(\mathcal E_q|_S) = \mathcal M_q\).
